title: North Carolina's 2nd Congressional District Election, 2026
description: The 2026 election for North Carolina's 2nd Congressional District will determine who represents most of Wake County, including much of Raleigh, in the U.S. House of Representatives. The district was redrawn in October 2025 as part of a mid-decade redistricting process. Incumbent Democrat Deborah Ross, first elected in 2020, is seeking a fourth term. The general election features four candidates: Ross, Republican nominee Eugene Douglass, Green Party nominee Michael Dublin, and Libertarian nominee Matthew Laszacs. This race takes place in a district that has historically leaned Democratic but faces new political dynamics after the 2025 redistricting and the open U.S. Senate race in North Carolina.
polling_note: No public general election polls were found for this race as of June 2026. The primary election was held on March 3, 2026.

candidates.name: Deborah K. Ross
candidates.summary: Deborah Ross is the incumbent U.S. Representative for North Carolina's 2nd Congressional District, first elected in 2020. She previously served in the North Carolina House of Representatives from 2003 to 2013 and worked as a civil rights attorney. In Congress, she serves on the House Judiciary Committee and the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, and is a Chief Deputy Whip. She has focused on healthcare access, clean energy, immigration reform, and women's rights, with 15 pieces of her legislation signed into law.

candidates.name: Eugene F. Douglass
candidates.summary: Eugene Douglass (also known as Gene Douglass) is the Republican nominee for North Carolina's 2nd Congressional District. He is a retired chemistry professor with over 30 years of teaching experience, holding a Ph.D. from North Carolina State University. He also holds an M.S. and an M.Div. and has worked as a consultant in specialty chemicals and Asperger's syndrome counseling. Douglass advanced to the general election without a primary opponent.

candidates.name: Michael L. Dublin Jr.
candidates.summary: Michael Dublin is the Green Party nominee for North Carolina's 2nd Congressional District. He is a teacher in a public school, a U.S. military veteran, and a native of Wake County. Dublin graduated from North Carolina State University. He previously ran for this seat in 2024 under the Green Party banner and is campaigning on a platform of "People, Planet, and Progress," emphasizing environmental justice, veterans' issues, and education funding.

candidates.name: Matthew F. Laszacs
candidates.summary: Matthew Laszacs (also known as Matt Laszacs) is the Libertarian Party nominee for North Carolina's 2nd Congressional District. He earned a Bachelor of Science degree from North Carolina Wesleyan College in 2009 and works as a director in charge of operations. Born in Philadelphia and raised in a military family, Laszacs moved to North Carolina in 2001. He has previously run for office as a Libertarian candidate for NC House District 41 and NC Senate District 14. He advocates for reducing occupational licensing, expanding school choice, and cutting taxes.

career_history.description: Director in charge of operations at a Raleigh-area company.

forecast.rationale: No public general-election polling is available for this race, so the forecast rests on non-polling indicators and should be treated cautiously. Deborah Ross is the three-term incumbent seeking a fourth term, giving her clear advantages in name recognition, fundraising, and institutional support. The district encompasses most of Wake County and much of Raleigh — historically Democratic-leaning suburban and urban territory. However, the district was redrawn in October 2025 via mid-decade redistricting, creating meaningful uncertainty about the exact partisan baseline. In addition, the open U.S. Senate race in North Carolina could alter turnout dynamics. The Republican nominee is a first-time candidate (retired chemistry professor who ran unopposed in the primary), while third-party candidates (Green, Libertarian) may pull small shares. On the available race data, Democrats are favored, but the absence of polling and the redistricting uncertainty preclude a 'safe' rating.
